query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: During moderate-temperature aging of a rapidly solidified Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy, nanoscale Al–Mg–rich intermetallic precipitates nucleate and grow, depleting the surrounding matrix in Mg and enriching it in Al; this microchemical partitioning (structural mediator) promotes the formation of a more continuous Al2O3 film during high-temperature oxidation (mechanism 1), lowering oxidation rate, while the discrete intermetallics serve as cathodic sites in aqueous chloride environments (mechanism 2), accelerating localized corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: As-quenched, non-equilibrium supersaturated solid solution containing randomly distributed Mg among Al, Cu, Zn, Gd and other HEA elements, with no or minimal discrete intermetallic phases.
generation.intervention: Isothermal annealing at 500 °C for 100 hours in air (for oxidation) and in inert atmosphere (for corrosion sample preparation).
generation.conditions: Aging temperature 500 °C ± 5 °C; exposure time 100 h ± 5 h; oxidation in flowing air at 1 atm; corrosion testing in 3.5 wt% NaCl at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale Al–Mg–rich intermetallic precipitates (e.g., Al3Mg2 or similar Laves-type phases) nucleated during aging.
generation.mechanism: (1) Depletion of Mg and enrichment of Al in the matrix enhances selective formation of a continuous, slow-growing Al2O3 scale during oxidation. (2) The dispersed intermetallics act as local cathode sites relative to the matrix, increasing anodic dissolution rates under chloride attack.
generation.predicted_outcome: After aging, oxidation mass gain at 500 °C for 100 h decreases by ~20% relative to as-quenched baseline; corrosion current density in 3.5 wt% NaCl increases by a factor of ~2 with more pronounced localized attack.
generation.baseline: As-quenched alloy shows higher oxidation mass gain (~60 mg/cm2) and lower corrosion current density (~5 µA/cm2) with mostly uniform corrosion.
generation.boundary: Valid for alloys of density <6 g/cm3 with similar Al:Mg ratio (Al-rich), for aging temperatures between 450–550 °C and times between 10–200 h; does not apply if aging leads to continuous brittle intermetallic network (>volume fraction 30%).
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of oxidation and corrosion changes may vary with exact precipitate volume fraction and distribution; microalloying additions (e.g., Gd, Zn) could modify precipitate chemistry.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the same alloy; one measured in the as-quenched condition, the other aged at 500 °C for 100 h in air. Characterize precipitate volume fraction by SEM/EDS and XRD. Perform TGA to assess oxidation mass gain. Conduct potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5 wt% NaCl to measure corrosion current density and map attack morphology by SEM.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If aged samples do not show both (a) ≥10% reduction in oxidation mass gain and (b) ≥1.5× increase in corrosion current density/pitting relative to as-quenched baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.
